Restaurant's favorite review
Elevated fine dining
Nov 2025 • Couples
Having previously dined at Kirk Westaway's two Michelin starred restaurant, JAAN, in Singapore, when we found out that he had opened a restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City and that we were staying at the hotel we knew we had to book. Located on the 23rd floor of the Hotel Des Arts Saigon, it has sweeping views over the city. The decor is refined and restrained, with timber parquetry floors, wood panelling on the walls, timber chairs with soft red velvet lining, white marble tables - it has the feel of a classic dining area at an exclusive English men's club. 

The menu reflects Westway's vision of reimagining traditional British classics, with a refined modern twist. Rather than going to the tasting menu, we decided to be more selective and chose from the ala carte options. We decided on the smoked beef tartare and the Albion tomato for starters, followed by the roasted duck and wagyu striploin. For dessert we opted for the lemon tart and the Calamansi. The Albion tomato is a different take on JAAN's heirloom tomato but just as delicious. The beef tartare was amazing. Both the meat dishes were cooked to perfection and I could not fault the lemon tart. 

The service was impeccable, and we appreciated head chef, Chris Clarke, taking the time to chat to us about our meal. 

If you are looking for a fine dining option in Ho Chi Minh City, then this is the place you have to try - thoroughly recommend it.

reviews.review_title: Review at The Albion By Kirk Westaway
reviews.review_text:
MEW
Melbourne, Australia90 contributions
1
From BAD to Worse.
Apr 2026 • Family
There are disappointing meals, and then there are evenings so laboriously self-important that disappointment gives way to irritation. Dining at The Albion by Kirk Westaway at M Gallery HCMC was not merely underwhelming, it was the sort of experience that leaves one feeling faintly rebuked for having expected anything better. Overpriced Rubbish.

This is, after all, a restaurant that arrives dressed for the role. It has the name, the positioning, the polished surfaces, the air of cultivated seriousness that suggests one is about to be treated to something urbane and exacting. It knows what sort of place it wishes to be seen as. The trouble is that wishing to be elegant and actually being elegant are quite different accomplishments, and The Albion seems to have mistaken the performance of refinement for the thing itself.

The room has that studied, upscale confidence so beloved of hotel dining rooms trying to transcend the fact that they are, in the end, hotel dining rooms. Everything is arranged to imply taste. Everything has been considered. Everything is trying just a little too hard. And yet the overall feeling is not of ease, nor charm, nor that seductive sense that you have placed yourself in expert hands. Rather, it is of entering a carefully managed fiction in which all the right signals are present, but very little actual pleasure has been allowed to survive the planning.

Service, which in a restaurant like this should function as the invisible architecture of the evening, was instead one of its more dispiriting weaknesses. Good service flatters without fawning, guides without interrupting, anticipates without hovering. It makes you feel not important exactly, but secure, as though the night is in the care of grown-ups. Here, one had the opposite sensation. The staff seemed trapped in that modern purgatory between friendliness and choreography, where everything is technically performed and yet nothing feels natural. Courses appeared with the solemnity of ritual but without the ease that gives ritual grace. Interactions had been started to be learned but not inhabited. It was service as recitation, not hospitality. Noting genuine about it.

And then, unhappily, there was the food. A great many restaurants now serve dishes that look as though they have been composed chiefly for the reassurance of the kitchen, each element carefully placed to demonstrate intention, rather than to advance flavour, appetite, or delight. The Albion appears to subscribe enthusiastically to this school. Plate after plate arrived bearing all the visible signs of effort, precision, and conceptual ambition, and yet the cumulative effect was oddly joyless. One can forgive simplicity if it is delicious, and extravagance if it is exhilarating, but earnest mediocrity presented as luxury is much harder to indulge.

The menu seems determined to persuade you that you are experiencing something thoughtful, elevated, perhaps even faintly important. But food does not become impressive because it is described reverently or delivered with a practiced murmur. It must still taste of something beyond intention. It must still justify its own existence. Too much here felt as though it had passed through committees of technique and aspiration only to arrive at the table stripped of appetite. There were textures, there were flourishes, there were little gestures toward cleverness, but precious little that made one want another bite for the simple, old-fashioned reason that it was genuinely pleasurable to eat.This is the particular disappointment of restaurants with grand ambitions and insufficient soul. If a modest neighbourhood bistro serves an imperfect dinner, one shrugs, pays, and moves on. But when a restaurant advertises itself as a serious player, when it asks for the money, the attention, and the expectation that accompany prestige, then it assumes a larger burden. It must not merely avoid failure, it must offer conviction. It must make the diner feel that the fuss was worth it. The Albion never came close.

Worst of all was the curious hollowness of the thing. Fine dining, or whatever phrase we are meant to use now, need not always be warm or rustic or overflowing with personality. But it must possess some animating spirit, some reason to exist beyond margin and branding. Here, one searched for that spirit and found only polish. The evening seemed assembled rather than hosted, engineered rather than imagined. You could see the mechanics of ambition everywhere, and that only made the absence of genuine generosity more glaring.

In the end, The Albion commits the gravest sin available to a restaurant of this sort: it is not outrageously bad, not gloriously absurd, not even memorably incompetent. It is simply expensive, self-conscious, and deadening, which is perhaps more unforgivable. At least catastrophe has the decency to entertain. This merely consumed time, money, and goodwill while insisting, with a straight face, that one ought to be impressed.

Ho Chi Minh City is full of places that understand something The Albion does not, namely that dining out should involve pleasure. Not branding, not theatre, not the hushed exchange of approved signals, but pleasure. One ought to leave a restaurant feeling fed, charmed, surprised, delighted, or at the very least cared for. To leave instead faintly irritated, still hungry for something more convincing, and calculating all the other better places one might have gone is a poor result by any standard. By the end of the evening, the chief emotion was not anger, exactly, but contempt for the waste of potential. The Albion does not fail because it lacks polish. It fails because it mistakes polish for excellence, and those are not remotely the same thing.
